extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theology, ecclesiology, and Hobbes's Leviathan (scholars, advanced undergraduates, general readers of early-modern political philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting interpretive standards and doctrinal/constitutional claims from Hobbes's discussion of salvation, hell, church, and sovereign authority in Leviathan. Focuses on Hobbes's definitions and arguments about the place of the Kingdom of God, nature of Hell, the Church, and sovereign rights deriving from Abraham and Moses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kingdom of God as a civil commonwealth on Earth
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kingdom of God is a Civil Common-wealth, where God himself is Sovereign; after the coming again of Christ to reign actually and eternally, 'the Kingdom of God is to be on Earth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues from Scripture (e.g., Isaiah, Joel, John, Acts) that salvation and the chief seat of God's kingdom will be in Jerusalem on Earth — 'Jerusalem, a quiet habitation' — and that God will reign from there; the name 'Kingdom of Heaven' may reflect God's throne being in Heaven, not that subjects ascend above God's footstool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascension, souls, and resurrection (when immortality begins)
rubrics_metrics.description: Immortality of man is not intrinsic to human nature but bestowed by God's will at the Resurrection; souls of the departed may be 'in Heaven' after death, but eternal life for man is reckoned from the Absolution/Resurrection, not natural immortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes distinguishes the soul's possible presence with God after death from the immortal life promised to the faithful at the Resurrection; scriptural texts (e.g., John 3:13, Luke 20:37-38, Job 14) are used to show that 'life' is reckoned from divine promise and the general Resurrection rather than from natural human essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal vs. metaphorical sense of scriptural language concerning Hell
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of Hell (fire, bottomless pit, lake of fire, under-earth, under-water, utter darkness, Gehenna/Tophet) are to be taken metaphorically rather than as literal geographic/topographical claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes reasons that scriptural references (Sodom's fire, Egyptian darkness, Valley of Hinnom) provide metaphors for destruction, disgrace, and separation from God's elect; since literal reading (e.g., a bottomless pit within Earth's globe) is implausible, the 'place' and 'nature' of Hellish torment should be sought in proper (metaphorical) senses grounded in the real conditions they signify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural depictions of Hell's torments as symbolic indicators of mental and bodily suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Torments are expressed variously — 'weeping and gnashing of teeth,' 'the worm of conscience,' 'fire,' 'shame and contempt' — and signify grief, discontent of mind, bodily pains, and calamity resulting from being deprived of eternal felicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes explains these phrases as metaphorical representations of the kinds of misery (mental distress, bodily suffering, shame, second death) that accompany exclusion from salvation; he distinguishes 'everlasting fire' (an enduring state of torment or destruction) from an eternal, undying life of the damned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tormenters (Satan, Devil, Abaddon) as offices/appellatives, not proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Names like 'Satan,' 'Devil,' and 'Abbadon' are appellatives indicating office or quality (Enemy, Accuser, Destroyer) rather than individuated proper names of supernatural persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes recommends translating these terms rather than leaving them as untranslated proper names; he uses this to argue that 'the Enemy' should be understood as the earthly enemies of God's kingdom (i.e., opposing political powers), so if God's kingdom is on Earth, the Enemy's kingdom is likewise earthly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and senses of 'Church' in Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'Church' (Ecclesia) has multiple senses: (1) God's House/Temple (metaphorical for congregation but used for edifices), (2) an assembly/called-together congregation (Ecclesia Legitima vs. Ecclesia Sugkechumene), (3) the people who have right to be of the congregation (the whole multitude of Christians), (4) a certain part of Christians (a local church), (5) the Elect only (Church Triumphant), and (6) a congregation assembled of professing Christians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes catalogues scriptural uses (1 Cor. 14; Acts; Ephes.; Matt. 18) and emphasizes that context determines sense; he stresses the legal/political dimension when 'Church' is taken as an assembly with authority to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/political definition of Church (Hobbes's formal definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes's definition: 'A CHURCH [is] a company of men professing Christian Religion, united in the person of one Soveraign; at whose command they ought to assemble, and without whose authority they ought not to assemble.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a normative criterion: a body counts as a Church (capable of corporate acts, law, absolution, condemnation) only if it is a lawfully constituted congregation under a civil sovereign's authority; unlawful assemblies are not legitimate Churches in this sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church and civil commonwealth identical in authority-capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the Church can command, judge, absolve, condemn, or do other acts as one person, it is the same as a Civil Common-wealth; there is no universal Church on Earth because no earthly power is universally sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues that temporall and spirituall government are not two separate lawful authorities on Earth; external acts of religion fall under the civil sovereign's jurisdiction; inward belief is not punishable by temporal law. He warns that without one chief pastor (i.e., sovereign authority), faction and civil war follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign rights deriving from Abraham's covenant (three consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: From God's covenant with Abraham Hobbes draws three points: (1) God spoke only to Abraham, so positive commandments of God for Abraham's family were received through Abraham as sovereign; (2) Abraham (and by analogy the sovereign) may punish those who claim private visions counter to the laws; (3) none but Abraham (and thus none but the civil sovereign) can determine what God said to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes reads the Abrahamic covenant as a model for political-religious authority: subjects without private revelation must obey their civil sovereign in external religious acts; private pretensions of revelation may be lawfully suppressed; sovereigns are the interpreters/judges of God's word for their commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign as sole interpreter of divine speech in the commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Just as Abraham alone could know and interpret what God spoke to him for his family, so the person who holds Abraham's place in a commonwealth (the sovereign) alone can take notice of and interpret what is or is not the Word of God for that commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is offered as a constitutional rule: interpretation of divine commands for the polity is a matter of sovereign competence; ecclesiastical autonomy of interpretation is thereby limited by civil authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redemption explained as ransom/oblation, not equivalent to full satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Redemption presupposes a ransom; but 'ransom' here does not mean a satisfaction equivalent to the offense (which no man could make), rather a sacrifice or oblation that God is pleased to accept; Christ's death is the sacrifice/oblation required by the Father for the Salvation at the second coming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes clarifies that forgiveness of sin can be gratis or on terms God accepts (e.g., sacrifices in the Old Testament); Christ's oblation is the acceptable price demanded by God, not a juridical purchase making sin 'vendible.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Salvation defined broadly as remission from sin and from misery/death
rubrics_metrics.description: In Scripture 'salvation' comprehends both remission of sin and deliverance from the evils that sin brought (want, sickness, death); to be 'saved' is to be secured either against particular evils or absolutely against all evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes uses scriptural examples (e.g., Mat. 9.2 regarding forgiveness and healing) to argue that pardoning sins and restoring health are conceptually united in the biblical notion of salvation; general salvation is the eternal state enjoyed after Judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of three 'worlds' in Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture refers to three worlds: the Old World (from Adam to the Flood), the Present World ('My kingdom is not of this world'), and the World to Come (the new heavens and new earth promised in 2 Peter, where Christ shall reign).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes uses this taxonomy to situate his interpretation of eschatology: 'the World to come' is where the elect will be gathered and Christ will reign everlastingly, under which the earthly aspect of God's kingdom and salvation are to be understood.
